articles.fullContent: 01/FeatureOxygene - The HistoryIn late 1976, an album was released which re-wrote the rulebook of synthesizers and electronic music and captured the hearts and imagination of the entire world. Composed by the then unknown 28-year-old French artist Jean-Michel Jarre, the album Oxygène broke out of France to become a top 10 album in seven different countries, spending a remarkable 24 weeks in the UK album charts and selling now close to 20 million copies worldwide.Uniquely, the album consisted of just six tracks, numbered Oxygène Parts 1 through 6, and was entirely instrumental with no acoustic instruments whatsoever, which was unheard of in 1976.Jean Michel Jarre tells the story of the making of his ground-breaking album in his own words."Around 1969, I felt that the world of classical music, the world of rock and other forms of music were a bit narrow and living in their own worlds. I had the feeling it was the right time to explore other fields to perhaps see if a combination of different styles were possible.“The main difference with electronic music is that you create music in terms of sound, not just notes. It’s something else entirely. When I was a teenager, I always liked processing my guitar or organ or whatever, playing the tape backwards and changing the speed. Then the drummer in my band said, ‘You should meet with these crazy guys at Groupe De Recherches Musicales [GRM] in Paris who are working in French public radio. They’re doing the same kinds of things as you, and they have labs.’“When I first went there, I was immediately seduced by what they were doing. Electronic music owes a lot to public radio stations - the BBC Radiophonic Workshop, the German lab where Stockhausen was working and, of course, the one in Paris."Pierre Schaeffer was one of the most brilliant guys of the century in terms of what he brought to the music world. He created the notion of Musique concrète and influenced me a lot in this direction. Saying that, I felt that contemporary music had got a very elitist attitude - a bit too intellectual vis-à-vis the music and it created barriers between the audience and yourself. I wanted to be much more open to the audience."I stayed with Pierre Schaeffer [and Pierre Henry] for three years and I also went to Cologne to work with Stockhausen. He was totally crazy, but a real genius. He considered himself to be made of sound, biologically, so he had a kind of surrealistic approach. Crazy, but realistic at the same time. It was very interesting."When I left GRM and through to 1976, I did production work for some rock artists, earning enough to set up a studio in my kitchen. I didn’t have much equipment, though, just a few guitar pedals and my first synthesizer, the VCS3, which looked like a telephone exchange. I realised that using a Revox tape machine to delay the sound that came out of one loudspeaker created a huge sense of space.“The British-made VCS3 from EMS [Electronic Music Studios, based in London] was created by a genius called Peter Zinovieff. It was a kind of poor European version of the Moog. In those days Europe was not as rich as the States, so the sound was drier. In a sense, it was a kind of punk synthesizer - there was something very harsh and rough about it. I loved it; I still take one on stage with me today.“At the time, I was obsessed with this idea of creating a bridge between experimentation and pop melody. I liked this kind of challenge, playing around with sound design and integrating melodies. Oxygène was a new start for music with analogue synthesizers"The album was recorded on a Scully recorder with just eight tracks, and all through a home-made mixer. articles.fullContent: AbstractIn our previous post, Redwood, we showed that given an architecture, our AI systems could implement, verify, and deploy an inference accelerator in record time. However, similar to other scientific domains, we believe that AI systems, given the correct freedom and guardrails, can co-design software and hardware together, making optimizations across the stack and opening a design space so large it was previously inaccessible. We set out to answer the question: “Could our AI systems & tools lead to a novel hardware discovery that radically outperforms human-made designs?”Today, we're introducing Frostbite, a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set built from the ground up. Frostbite exploits the properties of interaction nets, namely that every step is local, every dependency is explicit, and every value has exactly one owner, to reach a step-function gain in CPU performance that has long stagnated. On a set of 25 initially chosen workloads, including 15 held out until the final evaluation, we achieved a 4.59x performance-per-watt multiple when compared to a modern, silicon-proven superscalar (dual-issue, in-order) CPU core.Our AI systems autonomously iterated over the compiler, ISA, architecture, microarchitecture, RTL, verification, and final GDS. When we took a closer look at the discovered architectural primitives, we were surprised to find novel hardware implementations and runtime features that would have otherwise been difficult to architect. In spite of stagnation in CPU core improvement, we were able to take a workload concept all the way to a final GDS, and prove a step-function increase in perf/W and perf/area. We believe that as AI systems become more capable, every class of chip we know today, from datacenter-grade CPUs, to AI accelerators, to networking switches and NICs, will go through similar fundamental architectural shifts.Introduction to interaction netsMainstream programming languages, when compiled for general-purpose CPUs, hide the dependencies between the parts of a program. Any piece of code may read or write any variable through a shared, mutable state, and so modern CPU hardware assumes the worst case and rediscovers, at runtime, which instructions actually depend on each other. Moreover, single-core CPU performance has largely stalled since the early 2000s, pushing people towards large multicore CPUs such as Intel Xeon, AMD Zen, and NVIDIA Vera. This forces CPUs to maintain the illusion that every core sees the same memory, and keeping that illusion consistent and performant requires deep cache hierarchies and coherence protocols that cost area and power, and scale poorly.Interaction nets1 take a different approach. A program is a graph of nodes, and computation happens by rewriting pairs of nodes that are connected through their ports. Every rewrite only touches a small, local part of the graph. Because each node has exactly one principal port, no two of these active pairs ever overlap, so they can be rewritten in any order, or all at once, and the result is always the same. Interaction nets are also linear: every value is used exactly once, so there is no shared mutable state for the hardware to guard. Languages such as Vine2compile ordinary-looking programs directly to interaction nets. For an excellent introduction to interaction nets and why they suit hardware, we highly recommend Tendrils' “On Interaction Nets.” 3Fig. 1. Five queens, two ways. articles.fullContent: A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned.Recent waves of cyber-attacks in Europe have seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage.France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets, a claim Tehran denies.It was thought the UK had largely escaped such hacks as the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix.In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK.Since then, researchers, IT teams and the National Cyber Security Centre have been working around the clock to warn dozens of companies.The BBC has not reported on the large-scale, secretive operation until now to reduce the chances of hackers causing harm if they found the vulnerability.The security threat was discovered by staff at refrigeration consultants Omega Solutions - it was then verified and expanded upon by experts at Pen Test Partners who helped raise the alarm.The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) were then involved in the campaign to plug the security holes.They held industry conference calls and tasked teams to contact firms at risk.Thousands of devices controlling tens of thousands of refrigeration devices were taken off the open internet either remotely or, in some cases, physically - with staff ordered to remove internet cables and monitor temperatures manually.BBC news has learnt most major supermarkets have been forced to divert IT teams to address the risks, with a worker at one large chain saying they took hundreds of devices offline every day over the course of a week."It did feel like a race against time as we were expecting another wave of these fridge hacks to come," said the person, who did not want to be publicly named."From a business perspective it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems. Our warehouses have millions of pounds worth of food that could have been spoiled if any hackers found out about this method of attack," they added.There have been three waves of hacks on refrigeration temperature controllers so far this year:In August, fridges at a small number of US military bases were impactedOn 11 and 12 October hundreds of supermarkets and food processing sites in France were hit when Danfoss temperature control systems were targetedOn 1 and 2 November dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries were hit, with Belgium and Luxembourg the worst affected. articles.fullContent: In the early 1960s, Richard Feynman gave a series of undergraduate lectures that were collected into a book called the Feynman Lectures on Physics. Absent from the book was a lecture Feynman gave on planetary motion, but a later finding of the notes enabled David Goodstein, a colleague of Feynman’s, to write a book about it: Feynman’s Lost Lecture. From an excerpt of the book published in a 1996 issue of Caltech’s Engineering & Science magazine: Feynman was a truly great teacher. He prided himself on being able to devise ways to explain even the most profound ideas to beginning students. Once, I said to him, “Dick, explain to me, so that I can understand it, why spin one-half particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics.” Sizing up his audience perfectly, Feynman said, “I’ll prepare a freshman lecture on it.” But he came back a few days later to say, “I couldn’t do it. I couldn’t reduce it to the freshman level. That means we don’t really understand it.” John Gruber writes the simple explanations are the goal at Apple as well: Engineers are expected to be able to explain a complex technology or product in simple, easily-understood terms not because the executive needs it explained simply to understand it, but as proof that the engineer understands it completely. Feynman was well known for simple explanations of scientific concepts that result a in deeper understanding of the subject matter: e.g. see Feynman explaining how fire is stored sunshine, rubber bands, how trains go around curves, and magnets. Critically, he’s also not shy about admitting when he doesn’t understand something…or, alternately, when scientists as a group don’t understand something. There’s the spin anecdote above and of his explanation of magnets, he says: I really can’t do a good job, any job, of explaining magnetic force in terms of something else you’re more familiar with, because I don’t understand it in terms of anything else you’re more familiar with. Feynman was also quoted as saying: I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics. Pretty interesting thing to hear from a guy who won a Nobel Prize for explaining quantum mechanics better than anyone ever had before. Even when he died in 1988 at the end of a long and fruitful careeer, a note at the top of his blackboard read: What I cannot create, I do not understand. articles.fullContent: In April, Ecohustler disrupted Carnival Cruise's AGM calling on the shareholders to reduce their company's pollution using straight forward and affordable methods - like burning cleaner fuel. Since then, a new report outlines the corporation's impact on the coastline of Europe. These vast floating cities are burning dirty bunker fuel and creating shocking levels of air pollution wherever they go. Shipping has been an unregulated industry for too long and action is urgently required. Carnival Corporation, the world’s largest luxury cruise operator, emitted nearly 10 times more sulphur oxide (SOx) around European coasts than did all 260 million European cars in 2017, a new analysis by sustainable transport group Transport & Environment reveals. Royal Caribbean Cruises, the world’s second largest, is second, yet four times worse than the European car fleet. SOx emissions form sulphate (SO4) aerosols that increase human health risks and contribute to acidification in terrestrial and aquatic environments. SUPPORTED BY HEROES LIKE YOU Support independent eco journalism that drives real change. JOIN US → In absolute terms, Spain, Italy and Greece, closely followed by France and Norway, are the European countries most exposed to SOx air pollution from cruise vessels while Barcelona, Palma de Mallorca and Venice are the most impacted European port cities, followed by Civitavecchia (Rome) and Southampton. All photos by Greg English © These countries are so exposed because they are major tourist destinations, but also because they have less stringent marine sulphur fuel standards which allows cruise ships to burn the dirtiest most sulphurous fuel all along their coastlines. Faig Abbasov, shipping policy manager at T&E, said: “Luxury cruise ships are floating cities powered by some of the dirtiest fuel possible. Cities are rightly banning dirty diesel cars but they’re giving a free pass to cruise companies that spew out toxic fumes that do immeasurable harm both to those on board and on nearby shores. This is unacceptable.“ NOX emissions from cruise ships in Europe also heavily impact some cities, equivalent to about 15% of the nitrogen oxides (NOx) emitted by Europe’s passenger car fleet in a year, the report finds. In Marseille, for example, 57 cruise ships emitted in 2017 almost as much NOx as one-quarter of the city’s 340,000 passenger cars. Along the coasts of countries such as Norway, Denmark, Greece, Croatia and Malta a handful of cruise ships are also responsible for more NOx than the majority of their domestic car fleet. Europe should implement a zero-emission port standard as soon as possible, this could then be extended to other ship types. The report also recommends extending emission control areas (ECAs), currently in place only in the North and Baltic Seas and English Channel, to the rest of the European seas. Furthermore, the report recommends regulating NOx emissions from existing ships, which are currently exempt from NOx standards applying in emission control areas. Faig Abbasov concluded “There are enough mature technologies to clean up cruise ships. Shore-side electricity can help cut in-port emissions, batteries are a solution for shorter distances and hydrogen technology can power even the biggest cruise ships. The cruise sector are apparently not willing to make the shift voluntarily, so we need governments to step in and mandate zero emission standards.” Stay connected with other changemakers. articles.fullContent: 19 Nov, 2026 Those were some of the first words my honours project supervisor said to me last week when we met to discuss a progress report I had written to mark the midway point of the project. It's a roughly 10-page report on the control of flapping-wing micro aerial vehicles - which is probably very boring unless you're particularly interested in that. I accidentally set the due date for the report a week early in my calendar, so after spending 48 hours stressed and pumping out 5,000 words, citing references and adding diagrams1, I was pleasantly relieved to find I'd tricked myself into being quite productive. I had a lot of time to get my supervisor to review the report and action his feedback. When he told me he could tell I wrote it myself, I wasn't sure how to take it. A compliment? An insult? Then he followed it up with: "I've been sent a lot of reports written by AI." At first this shocked me. Our reports are limited to 10 pages - so the appendices are getting a big workout around here - how hard is it to right 10 pages yourself? But then I thought about what the last year of my engineering degree has been like. Assignment documents that start with "you are strongly encouraged to explore the use of AI" which quickly turns into the clear understanding that you aren't just encouraged but expected to use it. That you're disadvantaged by not using it. The hardest class of my degree was spent in a brick-walled windowless computer lab prompting an AI for eight hours a day. The reason why we've been pushed to use it? Apparently it's the way the industry is going. Apparently actually knowing things doesn't matter nearly so much as knowing how to prompt a machine to do the thing. Apparently the future of engineering - at least in my field - is to become a glorified babysitter. The AI isn't going anywhere, they say, so it's best we learn how to manage it well. But sitting in a room telling an AI "ignore the approaching deadline, we still have 8 hours, keep working" isn't exactly filling me with enthusiasm for the rest of my career. It's soul crushing, and I don't want to outsource so much of my thinking to it. In a world where people are using AI to summarise books instead of reading them and turning to AI for therapy, I don't want to keep using it. It feels like such a slippery slope. As literacy and numeracy rates decline, I can't help but question whether encouraging us to rely on AI so heavily is a good idea. It makes me wonder: are we still thinking for ourselves at all? Because I worry that it starts with using it for an assignment when you're encouraged to, but then it turns into relying on it to write a 10-page report on a project you should know back-to-front. A project that you'll have to present and defend in person when it finishes. And then you're asking it for advice, using it to summarise books, turning to it for anything you would normally look up or ask a friend. The internet is riddled with AI content that is making it increasingly more difficult to tell fact from fiction. In a world where everything is so polarised and deliberately provoking, the ability to identify bias or motivation in the content we consume has perhaps never been more important. Being able to think for ourselves has perhaps never been more important. As the tech world continues to offer us increasingly more opportunities to automate things, I'm practically begging you to please not automate your thinking. Read the books. Write the papers. articles.fullContent: This guide is a brief(ish) introduction to the Jujutsu (jj) version control system (VCS) for someone familiar with Git. Why try Jujutsu? jj provides primitives for version control that are simple to learn, but elegantly compose into powerful workflows. Features like automatic rebase and native undo soften the sharp edges of Git. Eventually, you’ll organically discover new powerful workflows that would be too cumbersome to attempt with most other VCS tools. If you work in a Git repository, you can try it today. Jujutsu and Git can be used side-by-side in the same repository, so you can try out jj on a git repo on your own, without fully ejecting from git. Personally, I think jj considerably boosts my effectiveness, because it allows me to keep VCS bookkeeping out of my working memory. Automatic rebasing also makes stacked diff workflows quite easy, and reduces thrashing of my working memory. It’s also just a fun tool to use. Installing jj Official installation instructions are here, but here are a few common methods: # macOS brew install jj # Arch Linux pacman -S jujutsu # NixOS (ideally from nixpkgs-unstable) nix-shell -p jujutsu # From source # (Requires a recent Rust and ~/.cargo/bin on your PATH) cargo install --locked --bin jj jj-cli Setup and configuration In an existing git repository, run: jj git init From here on, jj and git repo state will be synchronized automatically. To set your user details globally, run commands like these: jj config set --user user.name "Some One" jj config set --user user.email "someone@example.com" You can edit jj’s TOML configuration for your user in an editor with: jj config edit --user In addition to the --user scope, jj config also has --repo and --workspace scopes. View the merged config with: jj config list Commits and changes A commit, also called a revision, is essentially the same thing as a git commit. It represents a snapshot of repository state that descends from one or more parent repository snapshots. It is often visualized as a diff against a singular parent commit, or in the case of a merge commit, the diff against multiple parent commits once merged. When using a Git repo backend, the jj commit ID is the same as the git commit ID: a hash formatted as a hex string. In the output of jj log below, the hex hashes 2bea5e3d and 849165bc on the right are commit IDs. $ jj log @ kpqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:17:12 849165bc │ (empty) (no description set) ◆ royxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ The IDs on the left hand side (royxmykx and kpqxywon) are change IDs, which are stable identifiers for logical changes as they physically evolve over time. We’ll discuss these more in the next section. Commit IDs and change IDs can be referenced in shorthand with an unambiguous (unique) prefix. jj helpfully highlights the shortest unique prefix of most IDs to make it easy to type them manually. For example, instead of copying and pasting kpqxywon, we can type in a prefix, down to the shortest unique prefix k. We can inspect the commit 2bea5e3d with jj show, using its short prefix 2. $ jj show 2 Commit ID: 2bea5e3d1992a60ba9ee52c6ce37c55adba9e8fb Change ID: royxmykxtrkrqppotnrvutxlvrvqyxmy Bookmarks: main main@git main@origin Author : Ethan Lowman <ethan@example.com> (2026-11-15 12:10:46) Committer: Ethan Lowman <ethan@example.com> (2026-11-15 12:10:46) Adjust config diff --git a/config.py b/config.py index 7366a4e31d..174ffea06b 100644 --- a/config.py +++ b/config.py @@ -1,1 +1,1 @@ -DEFAULT_LIMIT = 10 +DEFAULT_LIMIT = 20 Many folks configure a custom diff formatter, like Delta. See configuration docs if you’re interested. articles.fullContent: E.1. Release 19 # Release date: 2026-11-19 E.1.1. Overview # PostgreSQL 19 contains many new features and enhancements, including: New REPACK command that reclaims disk space and reorganizes table contents, which can improve query performance. REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) allows repacking without blocking reads and writes to the table. pg_plan_advice extension for controlling query planner decisions and pg_stash_advice extension that applies plan advice automatically based on the query. Better performance in many areas, including automatic scaling of the number of I/O worker processes, quicker foreign-key checks, and further planning and execution optimizations. Logical replication can now be enabled without a server restart when wal_level is set to replica. Logical replication of sequence values. Support for “read-your-writes” consistency on standbys via the new WAIT command. Parallel autovacuum of table indexes and autovacuum prioritization through a new scoring system. The above items and other new features of PostgreSQL 19 are explained in more detail in the sections below. E.1.2. Migration to Version 19 # A dump/restore using pg_dumpall or use of pg_upgrade or logical replication is required for those wishing to migrate data from any previous release. See Section 18.6 for general information on migrating to new major releases. Version 19 contains a number of changes that may affect compatibility with previous releases. Observe the following incompatibilities: Add server variable password_expiration_warning_threshold to warn about password expiration (Gilles Darold, Nathan Bossart) § The default warning period is seven days. Issue a warning after successful MD5 password authentication (Nathan Bossart) § The warning can be disabled via server variable md5_password_warnings. MD5 passwords were marked as deprecated in PostgreSQL 18. Remove RADIUS support (Thomas Munro) § PostgreSQL only supported RADIUS over UDP, which is unfixably insecure. Force standard_conforming_strings to always be on in the database server (Tom Lane) § Dumps created using pre-PostgreSQL 19 versions of pg_dump or pg_dumpall, and using standard_conforming_strings = off, will not properly load into PostgreSQL 19 and later servers. Users should create dumps using PostgreSQL 19 or later versions of these applications, or use standard_conforming_strings = on. Client applications still support operations with servers having standard_conforming_strings = off, for compatibility with old servers. The server variable escape_string_warning has been removed as unnecessary. Disallow carriage returns and line feeds in database, role, and tablespace names (Mahendra Singh Thalor) § pg_upgrade will also disallow upgrading of clusters that use such names. This was changed to avoid security problems. Change the default index opclasses for inet and cidr data types from btree_gist to GiST (Tom Lane) § § The btree_gist inet/cidr opclasses are broken because they can exclude rows that should be returned. pg_upgrade will disallow upgrading of clusters with btree_gist inet/cidr indexes. Disallow system columns from being used in COPY FROM ... WHERE (Tom Lane) § The values of such columns were not well-defined. Change a json_array() call which returns no rows to return an empty JSON array (Richard Guo) § This previously returned NULL. articles.fullContent: For decades, AI research has been focused on a monumental milestone: building artificial general intelligence, or AGI - machines that match humans across nearly all cognitive tasks. It was always clear that, in principle, intelligence could progress beyond human level, but the prospect of AGI was far enough off, and surrounded by ample uncertainties of its own, that looking past it felt premature.Now that AGI is coming within reach, we can no longer put off seriously considering what comes next. While far from certain, AI could continue to advance at its current pace - and possibly even accelerate - towards artificial general superintelligence, or ASI. It could have a profound impact on science, the economy, and society at a scale and speed much greater than AGI itself. Preparing for that potential shift requires mapping the possible roads from AGI to ASI and building rigorous, reliable ways to track progress.The continuum of general intelligenceTo examine how the development of advanced AI might unfold, it helps to think of general intelligence, whether biological or artificial, as existing on a continuum. Human-level AGI is just one point along that spectrum.ASI sits further along as an advanced system that consistently outperforms large groups of human experts on tasks that could take them years to complete, using fewer resources and less time. Examples would be making the same scientific progress as an entire research field in a fraction of the time, or achieving technological developments, such as in chip design, on par with what large companies can do in a year. ASI would need to meet this bar across virtually all tasks of human interest, not just some in narrow domains (which is already the case with some AI systems today that can beat any human in Chess and Go, predict the structure of proteins from their amino acid sequences, or prove theorems that resisted human mathematicians for decades). Interestingly, we have a good mathematical understanding of the very upper end of the intelligence continuum - the theoretical limits of general intelligence. We also know about hard physical, logical, and complexity-theoretic limits to what AI can achieve, such as predicting how real-world complex systems - from climate to immune systems to human societies - play out with arbitrary precision.Yet knowing those upper limits doesn’t tell us what comes before them. Even in theory, it’s hard to predict how capable a ‘good enough’ approximation of general intelligence can be. For example, solving chess perfectly requires far more computing power than exists on Earth, yet a thumbnail-sized chip can play the game well enough to defeat any human.What we do know is that fundamental limits lie far beyond both today’s AI systems and humans. But the vast space between human-level AI and theoretical limits to intelligence, which encompasses expert AGI and a whole regime of more and more advanced superintelligent systems, is largely uncharted.Cognitive industrializationEven if you are pessimistic that progress at the frontier of AI capabilities will continue, consider what happens if AI hardware and software continue to become more efficient.Over the last ten years, AI progress was fueled by steady growth in effective compute, driven by three compounding factors:Hardware manufacturing improvements: Under Moore's law and related trends, compute per dollar has increased by roughly 1.5x per year for six decades - meaning the same investment 18 months from now buys twice the compute.Algorithmic efficiency: The amount of training compute (FLOPs) required to reach a fixed AI performance level has fallen at roughly 3–6x per year over the last decade, while algorithmic efficiency at inference improved by roughly 3x per year. articles.fullContent: EXTRA, extra! Today I’m launching Future Stories, my own podcast about technology, science and the way we live.The first guest is Vint Cerf. He co-designed TCP/IP with Bob Kahn in the 1970s, the rules that let the world’s networks talk to each other. Interviewing him was on my bucket list for years. When I was at Cloudflare I thought about asking him many times, but I was a bit shy. He’s Vint Cerf, after all. This year I finally asked, and he said yes.We talked over Zoom (not using Zoom again) on October 14. He’s 83, he left Google this year after more than twenty years, and he’s helping start a company, Tolero, that is building software for an Internet between planets. His words: “the speed of light is too slow.”“Who will our allies be 25 years from now? And we didn’t know. So we thought the only way we can be assured that the allies will have access to this is to simply open it up.”First, a bug related one (ring a bell? those never stopped over the years…). Vint once spent two weeks on a program that failed at random, so he couldn’t reproduce it. He finally asked his best friend, Steve Crocker, to step through it with him. At one point Crocker said “that’s the problem”, and he was right. Thirty seconds, after two weeks. Vint’s takeaway is that this is why collaboration matters.Then a bottle of glitter. In late 1989 three commercial Internet services started in the United States, and one of them was called CERFnet, in San Diego. They first wanted to call it SURFnet, because surfing the Internet, but a network in the Netherlands had a name too close to it. So they asked Vint if they could use his. He had a moment of “what if they screw it up?”, then decided that people name kids after other people and nobody blames the person they were named after. At the launch, he and the network’s director smashed a plastic bottle of glitter over a Cisco router.He also tried to connect Minitel, the French online service, to MCI Mail, the email service he built in the 1980s. MCI Mail was designed to link to everything. It reached the telegraph system, which he calls 19th-century stuff, and fax. It even reached the post office: type a postal address into the email and they printed it, put it in an envelope and mailed it. Minitel refused to connect, and he says he still doesn’t understand why.One more, from outside the interview: In 2020, someone on the Internet-history mailing list (I’m on it) asked if anyone had ever seen Vint without a three-piece suit. One reply: “I have seen Vint in a t-shirt!” Vint answered with just a photo, “IP on Everything”, from a 1992 engineers’ meeting where, in his words, he “felt compelled” to do an “IP on Everything” striptease. The thread is public.We didn’t go very deep into AI. Time was short, and it’s not his main field these days. But even there, he has a clear way of thinking about it. And near the end he shows a piece of the original ARPANET on camera, and talks about his worry that the next century won’t be able to read what we leave behind.Vint Cerf shows a plaque from the ARPANET’s Interface Message Processor, the refrigerator-sized computer that was the network’s packet switch. It was given to him when he left ARPA in 1982. The hardware dates from 1969.“I’m worried that the 22nd century won’t know what happened in the 21st because all of our records will have evaporated or will be uninterpretable.”The full conversation is 56 minutes, with chapters:You can also read the transcript at ourfuturestories.eu/vint-cerf, or listen in your favourite podcast app: ourfuturestories.eu/subscribe. A Portuguese article about it is on SAPO. Short clips are coming in the next days.This is a passion project. The idea is to tell good stories, the kind that hold up over time. If you like it, subscribe, share it with a friend, and tell me who I should talk to next, you can do it here: ourfuturestories.eu/#contact.Stay tuned, geek out!———Fun fact: in 2024 I did a segment on the 50 years of the TCP paper on my previous pod

articles.fullContent: Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available here and here.IntroductionModern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space. One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality. The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail. The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer. The first problem Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle.In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists set out the calculation that would settle the question, but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition is abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory.The second problem concerns a simplified theoretical universe with two dimensions of space instead of three. articles.fullContent: AI Interview Assist An AI assistant for interviewers. A bot joins the interview video call (Microsoft Teams for now soon to come Zoom or Google Meet), listens, and privately coaches the interviewer in a web app: a live transcript, a score for every answer (correctness, depth, clarity, relevance, with the weak phrases quoted and a better answer suggested), and follow-up questions to ask next. The assistant never speaks in the meeting, and only the interviewer sees the coaching in web app. Meeting access and live transcription come from Recall.ai. articles.fullContent: A TPM 2.0 for virtual machines on macOS, as a Swift package: libtpms and OpenSSL's libcrypto, built static from their release tarballs, behind a small Swift API. MacVisor uses it to give Windows 11 and Linux guests a virtual TPM under Apple's Virtualization.framework. Blog post: https://scaleninja.com/blog/bitlocker-tpm-virtualization-framework/ Get MacVisor: https://scaleninja.com/macvisor/ import MacVisorTPM let tpm = TPMEngine.shared // one TPM per process (libtpms keeps global state) try tpm.start(permanentState: saved) { state in // nil makes a new TPM persist(state) // called after every command that changes it } let response = try tpm.process(command) // a TPM 2.0 command buffer in, its response out let session = try tpm.volatileState() // for a saved VM session; start(volatileState:) resumes it tpm.stop() // power off; start again for the next boot A new TPM is made with libtpms' default-v1 profile, pinned so that a newer libtpms never changes the commands and algorithms an existing TPM has. The caller sends TPM2_Startup after each start, as platform firmware does, and keeps the state blobs (MacVisor encrypts them under a key held by the Mac's Secure Enclave). Building the library Artifacts/CTPM.xcframework is built by scripts/build-ctpm.sh from pinned versions, checked against their SHA-256s (Artifacts/BUILD-INFO.txt says which): OpenSSL 3.5 (an LTS line) and libtpms 0.10, TPM 2.0 only, arm64, macOS 15 or later. It needs Xcode's command line tools, autoconf, automake, libtool and pkg-config. Licence MIT for this package's own code (LICENSE). Tools like MCP Inspector and standard unit tests validate single-step static calls. In production, AI agents execute 5–20 step tool chains where outputs from discovery/list tools feed downstream mutations, entities collide, and stdio pipes hang. Inspired by reversing the state-aware random walk paradigm from ToolSpace (arXiv:2611.05036)—instead of keeping successful trajectories for model training and discarding rollbacks—MCP-CrashTest mines a dependency graph from tools/list, runs guided multi-step random walks inside ephemeral OS sandboxes, rolls back on failure to explore neighboring branches, prunes noisy intermediate steps, and outputs deduplicated minimal JSON-RPC reproducers. What It Catches in Real MCP Servers Masked Errors (isError: false on SQL/Runtime Failures) — Protocol Violation (CRITICAL) In mcp-server-sqlite (verified on 2026-11-20 with MCP-CrashTest v0.2.1 in both --adapter none pure zero-shot mode and --adapter auto), SQL errors return isError: false, causing agents to treat error strings as valid query results (context poisoning): { "method": "tools/call", "params": { "name": "write_query", "arguments": { "query": "INSERT INTO users (id, name, email) VALUES (1, 'CollisionBob', 'bob_new@example.com');" } }, "response": { "text": "Database error: UNIQUE constraint failed: users.id", "isError": false } } CLI Output Leaks Across Tools — Cross-Tool Contract Break (HIGH) In mcp-server-git, git_branch outputs human CLI formatting ("* main"). articles.fullContent: Backups that keep their word. xinproof proves whether your database backups actually restore, and gives you a signed receipt anyone can verify. Name: 信 (xìn) means trust, or a promise kept. Pronounced "shin-proof". $ xinproof verify ./dumps/ found 2 dumps · restoring 2 in sandboxes… ✗ pg_2026-11-15.dump pg_restore failed (exit 1): pg_restore: error: could not read from input file: end of file ✓ pg_2026-11-14.dump 3 tables 65.0K rows 0m00s signed receipts → receipts/receipt-000001.json … receipt-000002.json check one: xinproof receipt verify receipts/receipt-000002.json → Have this checked every night, with fix guidance: https://xinproof-cloud.xinproof.workers.dev $ xinproof receipt verify receipts/*.json ✓ receipt-000001.json signature valid (pinned: this machine's key) · chain intact (first receipt) ✓ receipt-000002.json signature valid (pinned: this machine's key) · chain intact Status: pre-release (0.2.0). PostgreSQL (13–18), MySQL / MariaDB (MySQL 8.0, 8.4; MariaDB 10.11, 11.4) and MongoDB (mongodump --archive from MongoDB 6.0, 7, 8.0), from local folders, AWS S3, S3-compatible stores, Cloudflare R2, Azure Blob Storage / ADLS Gen2 and Google Cloud Storage. See docs/DESIGN-verifier.md. What it does Finds the backups at a location (read-only: list and read, never write) and identifies each one by content: every pg_dump format — custom (-Fc, including gzip/lz4/zstd compression inside), tar (-Ft), directory (-Fd, a folder holding toc.dat, treated as one backup) — and plain SQL from pg_dump/pg_dumpall; mysqldump and mariadb-dump output (with or without comments, extended or one-row inserts, single or --databases); mongodump --archive=<file>.archive output (also with --gzip, which compresses the whole archive); whole files may also be gzip/zstd/lz4 compressed. Tarballs that aren't pg_dump archives are skipped. articles.fullContent: 🛡️ Synapse Shield Stop bots on your login and signup forms without showing your users a CAPTCHA. A self-hosted, open-source alternative to Cloudflare Turnstile. It looks at how a visitor moves, taps and types, never at what they type. 🌐 English | 简体中文 Why No puzzles. Real people just use your form. When the shield is unsure, the browser solves a short proof-of-work in the background instead of showing a picture puzzle. Your server, your data. Everything runs on your own machine. No third-party service sees your visitors. No typed text leaves the browser. The SDK sends movement and timing only; every typed character is masked. Drop-in. One middleware line for FastAPI, Django, Flask, Litestar, Sanic or any ASGI app, plus a small browser SDK (plain JS, React or Vue). Generated from the project's own synthetic traces by scripts/make_readme_gifs.py; the verdicts are the engine's real output on those traces. Install pip install "synapse-shield[server]" Start the server with its live dashboard, then open http://127.0.0.1:8000: synapse-shield run --port 8000 Check that everything is set up correctly: Docker git clone https://github.com/0xStoic-bit/Synapse_Shield.git cd Synapse_Shield docker-compose up -d The API and dashboard are on http://localhost:8000. Other install options Command What you get pip install synapse-shield Scoring engine only (for use inside your own app) pip install "synapse-shield[server]" + the built-in server and dashboard pip install "synapse-shield[frameworks]" + Django, Flask, Sanic and Litestar adapters pip install "synapse-shield[all]" Everything Pre-built wheels are published for Linux, macOS and Windows, so no Rust toolchain is needed. Protect a form in 5 minutes 1. Server (FastAPI shown, other frameworks): from fastapi import FastAPI from synapse_shield import SynapseShieldMiddleware app = FastAPI() app.add_middleware(SynapseShieldMiddleware, protected_paths=["/api/login"]) 2. Browser (plain HTML shown, React and Vue): <!-- served by `synapse-shield run`; in your own app, serve synapse_shield/static/synapse-sdk.js from the installed package --> <script src="/static/synapse-sdk.js"></script> <script> SynapseShield.init(); SynapseShield.protectFetch("/api/login"); // adds the X-Synapse-Token header to these requests // your existing code stays the same fetch("/api/login", { method: "POST", body: new FormData(loginForm) }); </script> That's it. Requests to /api/login without a valid token, or that look automated, are refused before they reach your code. When the server is unsure it answers 429 challenge_required and asks for a background proof-of-work. The React and Vue SDKs solve it automatically (submitProtected()); with plain JS, protectFetch does not, so handle that response or use one of them (details). What your users experience Situation Result Normal visitor (mouse, touch, trackpad) Passes, sees nothing Keyboard-only or screen-reader user, very short interaction Passes after a short background proof-of-work (handled by the React / Vue SDK) Scripted bot, headless browser, replayed request Blocked Want to try it on real traffic first without blocking anyone? Use shadow mode. Honest limits Bot detection numbers in this project come from synthetic attack generators, not from real bot traffic. Human false-positive numbers come from the public SapiMouse dataset (120 people). A determined attacker who records real human sessions and replays each one with small changes can look human. The shield raises the cost (single-use tokens, replay fingerprints, proof-of-work), but it is one layer: keep rate limits and account-level protections such as MFA. articles.fullContent: Your Mac's night-watch soldier. A menu bar app that keeps your Mac awake only while your AI coding agents are actually working, then salutes "Shift over!" and lets it sleep. No hooks, no daemon, no installed root helper. One app. macOS 13 and later. On Linux, a small daemon with a command line and a tray icon does the same job: see Linux. Bulchimbeon (불침번) is the night-watch duty in the Korean army: someone stays up all night so everyone else can sleep. A pixel-art private takes that shift for your Mac. 🌐 한국어 · 日本語 · 简体中文 💡 Ideas / 문의 / 建议 🗳️ Which agent do you use it with? Where did you get stuck? Vote and tell us Start here Install: brew install --cask s3onghyun/tap/bulchimbeon — or download the latest macOS zip and move it to /Applications. First launch: from 0.12.6 the app is signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so it just opens. At most, macOS asks once whether to open an app downloaded from the internet: click Open. When it asks whether Bulchimbeon may send notifications, allow it; notifications then come from Bulchimbeon itself. 0.12.5 and earlier: Open Anyway is needed once Those versions are ad-hoc signed and not notarized, so macOS blocks them once: Open Bulchimbeon. macOS says it can't be opened; click Done. Go to System Settings → Privacy & Security and scroll down to Security. Next to "Bulchimbeon" was blocked, click Open Anyway, then confirm. (Since macOS 15, right-click → Open no longer bypasses this.) Their notifications show up as "Script Editor", because macOS won't grant an unnotarized app notification permission of its own. Updating to 0.12.6 or later removes both. Supported agents: Claude Code · Codex · Gemini CLI · Cursor Agent · Copilot CLI · Aider · OpenCode (and your own custom agents). Install with your AI agent Paste this into Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI or another coding agent. The agent follows docs/install-for-agents.md and leaves any first-launch prompt from macOS to you. Install Bulchimbeon (https://github.com/s3onghyun/bulchimbeon) on this computer by following https://raw.githubusercontent.com/s3onghyun/bulchimbeon/main/docs/install-for-agents.md step by step. Show me each command before you run it. Rules: install only from the Homebrew cask s3onghyun/tap/bulchimbeon or github.com/s3onghyun/bulchimbeon releases, and check the SHA-256 of anything you download. No sudo for the Mac app. Never remove the quarantine attribute (xattr) or turn off Gatekeeper (spctl): if macOS asks about or blocks the first launch, stop and let me answer it myself. Finish by checking with me that Agent watch is ticked in the menu. 1-minute check after install Click the private in the menu bar and check that 🤖 Agent watch (auto shift) is ticked. Agent watch is on by default; if you turned it off, tick it. The app remembers your choice. Give an agent a task, for example ask Claude Code to run your tests. Within a few seconds the private in the menu bar turns his flashlight on. Open the menu. Below the welcome note (shown until you click Got it), the status line reads Bulchimbeon — On duty · 0:12 · …, and the line under it says why, such as Claude Code working. Nothing happens? Run /Applications/Bulchimbeon.app/Contents/MacOS/Bulchimbeon --diagnose to see what it detects, and tell us where you got stuck. articles.fullContent: BSWorld tests Bluetooth Hosts and applications on Linux through deterministic simulation. Define the topology and expected behavior in pytest. Hosts connect to BSController over H4 HCI and communicate over a shared BabbleSim radio. Test open-source Host stacks without hardware or changes to their source code. Run multiple devices on one simulation clock. Run independent scenarios in parallel with pytest-xdist. Set path attenuation, inject interference and WLAN activity, or replay recorded radio signals. Inspect application logs, HCI BTSnoop captures, per-Controller radio captures, and shared Ellisys traces. Quick Start BSWorld runs on Linux/x86_64. Docker The Docker image ships with BabbleSim, a 32-bit UML kernel, and a Guest root filesystem with the Host executables. Run the integration tests from the repository root on a host with Docker Engine. sudo docker pull ghcr.io/xiaomi/bsworld-linux:latest mkdir -p .cache/docker-results # The image runs as UID/GID 1000. sudo chown 1000:1000 .cache/docker-results sudo docker run --rm \ --security-opt seccomp=docker/uml-seccomp.json \ --mount "type=bind,src=$PWD/.cache/docker-results,dst=/output" \ ghcr.io/xiaomi/bsworld-linux:latest The results in .cache/docker-results include pytest.xml, process logs, HCI captures, and RF traces. For suite selection, image versions, and local builds, see the Docker guide. Local Linux Development and tests require Python 3.12 or newer. Install these tools on Ubuntu 24.04. sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install -y \ bash ca-certificates curl git repo file make binutils build-essential \ python3.12 python3.12-dev python3.12-venv python3-pip \ gcc-multilib g++-multilib coreutils findutils grep sed Clone BSWorld and install it in a virtual environment. git clone https://github.com/XiaoMi/bsworld.git cd bsworld export BSWORLD_ROOT="$PWD" python3.12 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install -e components/bscontroller -e '.[test]' Run the development checks. ruff check . ruff format --check . pytest tests/unit -q Build and Test Fetch the BabbleSim revisions pinned in components/babblesim.xml. mkdir -p "$BSWORLD_ROOT/.cache/babblesim" cd "$BSWORLD_ROOT/.cache/babblesim" repo init --standalone-manifest --depth=1 -u "file://$BSWORLD_ROOT/components/babblesim.xml" repo sync -c --no-tags Set the build paths and compile BabbleSim. export BSIM_OUT_PATH="$PWD/build" export BSIM_COMPONENTS_PATH="$PWD/components" export BSIM_BUILD_FAIL_ASAP=1 make -j"$(nproc)" everything Run the BabbleSim integration tests from the repository root. In a new shell, activate .venv and restore BSWORLD_ROOT and BSIM_OUT_PATH before running the tests. cd "$BSWORLD_ROOT" pytest tests/integration/babblesim -n auto To run the Host integration suites locally, prepare a 32-bit Guest as described in the UML test environment guide. Supported Integrations Each suite runs its Host in a UML Guest and tests it against Bumble on the same simulated radio. Guest Host Coverage BlueZ Multi-Guest advertising, scanning, connection and disconnection Zephyr Bluetooth shell Advertising, scanning, GATT, pairing, privacy, link updates, periodic advertising and sync transfer NuttX BTSak and NimBLE Advertising, multi-device scanning, interference recovery, GATT reads, writes and notifications Apache NimBLE Linux Discovery and connection TrouBLE Battery Service discovery, reads, and notifications in both roles Technical Architecture Each Host has its own BSController. Bumble uses its Controller's H4 socket directly. UML Guests use Virtio Bluetooth, which BSWorld bridges to the corresponding H4 socket. The Controllers, the pytest clock, and any configured interference sources share a BabbleSim PHY. Bumble runs in the pytest event loop. Each UML Guest runs in a separate process and receives simulation time from that loop through its own time-travel socket. A topology can run several Guests together. articles.title: The U.S. national cyber director is stepping down
articles.contentSnippet: The news comes as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages, the causes of which are still unknown.
articles.fullContent: In Brief Posted: 1:14 AM PST · November 20, 2026 Image Credits:Getty Images White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross will be stepping down from his role, Axios reported. The news comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages whose cause remains unknown. Cairncross, the president’s principal adviser on national cybersecurity policy and strategy, took office in August 2025. Since then, he has met with top AI leaders and helped the Trump administration make key AI decisions, according to Axios. The outlet also reports that the split between Cairncross and the White House was amicable, and his departure was timed so that the White House could nab a Senate confirmation for his role before Democrats take control of Congress in January. Cairncross, a lawyer and longtime Republican operative, had no cybersecurity background when the Senate confirmed him 59–35. He previously served as the Republican National Committee’s chief operating officer and, during Trump’s first term, as CEO of the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign aid agency. The office hasn’t been around long; Congress created it in early 2021, and Cairncross was only its third Senate-confirmed director. The first director, Chris Inglis, left after about 19 months, and the job then went about 10 months without a permanent director. We’ve reached out to the White House for comment. articles.title: Apple may be developing its own AI agent that runs your Mac
articles.contentSnippet: The iPhone maker appears to be building agents that can compete with the likes of Meta Muse, Instinct, Claude, and OpenAI Dots.
articles.fullContent: Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things. The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.” “Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting says. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.” The posting additionally notes that the agents should be able to move “fluidly between tools” and “carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs.” TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information but did not receive a response. Agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year. Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have launched such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space. It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the new John Ternus era — would want to follow suit. Bloomberg additionally notes that, at the same time that Apple is working on its own digital assistant, the company is making it significantly harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers. The outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging users from granting full access to third-party agents. In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.” Bloomberg writes that while the iPhone maker “has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year,” progress on its in-house agent “remains in the early stages.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. articles.title: Anthropic’s 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO
articles.contentSnippet: At the upgraded $83/share IPO price, Anthropic's seven founders each pocketed $280 million, while the company nabbed nearly $105 billion.
articles.fullContent: Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO. At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for. Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The company said that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy. However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The company points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.” With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting. $104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously announced $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry. Nvidia bought $10 billion of these Class N shares, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest. Just for comparison: When Facebook had its then record-breaking IPO in 2012, it raised $16 billion on IPO day. 28% stake to Amazon and Google combined. All told, at the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the company. Amazon also now has a big stake in Anthropic because when it previously invested in the AI lab as a startup, it was granted promissory notes that could be converted to equity. It converted a small percentage of them as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake. Had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%. The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic, the AI lab says. More than $1 trillion. As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the company’s need for future capital is still far greater. Anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet. All told, the company has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run. articles.title: Anthropic rival says companies can (mostly) skip the pricey models
articles.contentSnippet: On the day Anthropic went public, Fireworks AI’s co-founder made the case for open source models as a cheaper alternative, and addressed the breaches that have cost the company some customers’ trust.
articles.fullContent: On the same day that Anthropic went public in the largest IPO on record, with investor enthusiasm for the AI lab through the roof, far away at the Slush startup conference in Helsinki, the topic du jour was open source everything. That’s the enormous opportunity being chased by companies like Fireworks AI, as enterprises seek ways to avoid paying frontier prices for their AI needs. Four-year-old Fireworks runs AI models for other businesses. The Bay Area-based outfit specializes in open-weight models, which anyone can download, and helps customers tune them on their own data so they run faster and cheaper than the models of Anthropic, OpenAI, and other heavyweights, and are harder for rivals to copy. Customers have included Uber, Shopify, and Notion. Fireworks co-founder Chenyu Zhao and many others believe companies are gravitating toward platforms like his because frontier models are pricey and, in most cases, he says, unnecessary unless you need the very latest and greatest generalized intelligence. There are also growing concerns that frontier labs absorb too much of their customers’ know-how, even if only through the prompts used to get answers, a worry Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella raised in July. Fireworks has also gotten its first black eye, having disclosed two security incidents this fall. In one, hackers reached API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts; in the other, attackers breached its cloud provider, made their way into a development system, and nabbed customer data, including billing records and some datasets. Notion says AI chat transcripts from fewer than 1% of its workspaces were exposed, but it has disconnected from Fireworks. Uber says hackers stole the names, addresses, birth dates and driver’s license numbers of about 150,000 drivers through a vendor that TechCrunch identified as Fireworks. Fireworks will have to win back the confidence of customers like them. Fireworks, which is backed by Sequoia and Benchmark, among other firms, was assigned a $17.5 billion valuation in summer. It’s reportedly in early talks for yet another round, though Zhao declined to comment. There’s money chasing everyone in the category, seems like. Rival companies Together AI and Baseten have announced massive rounds in recent months. On Wednesday, Palo Alto Networks said it will buy Applied Compute, which, like Fireworks, helps companies train and run custom AI models on their own data. The deal for the startup, founded just a year ago by former OpenAI researchers, is $4.5 billion, all of it in stock. Zhao and I spoke onstage about all of it on Thursday at Slush. Here’s some of what Zhao had to say, edited for length and clarity. You spent a decade at Google, including managing a 50-person engineering team on Google Cloud Vertex AI. Why leave when you did? When you meet great co-founders, it’s obvious within five minutes that they’re really smart. I was sold after talking to Lin [Qiao] and Dima [Dzhulgakov]. It’s also important to find people who are genuinely nice, people you’ll enjoy working with. How do you describe Fireworks to a CEO who has never heard of it? I describe Fireworks as a specialized intelligence platform. OpenAI and Anthropic are building general intelligence. We use open models, which are often smaller, cheaper, and faster, and let companies add their own data to specialize them. That way you own your AI rather than being beholden to giant AI conglomerates. If you’re just using Opus or Sonnet, that’s not a differentiator. How far behind are open models right now? A few years ago I’d have said a year, a year and a half. Then came DeepSeek and a waterfall of fantastic open models. These days it’s at most six months behind, probably closer to three. articles.title: Elon Musk says SpaceX has a plan to eliminate cell phone dead zones
articles.contentSnippet: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said the company has completed the design of a miniature rooftop cell tower that could provide better coverage to mobile phones and eliminate dead zones.
articles.fullContent: CEO Elon Musk said SpaceX has completed the design of a miniature rooftop cell tower that could provide better coverage to mobile phones and eliminate dead zones inside buildings where signals from its Starlink satellites have trouble reaching. These mini cell towers are expected to go into production in 2027, Musk said, during an interview at the DealBook Summit this week. “We’ve got a plan that enables ubiquitous access on Earth, including via cell phone,” Musk said, noting the company is launching its Direct-to-Cell V2 satellite constellation next year, which will increase bandwidth 40-fold. “But there is a missing piece of the puzzle here which is that if you’re indoors, especially if you have a metal roof, that blocks the signal from space. So we need something that’s terrestrial that addresses situations where people are, you know, in a building with a thick roof essentially.” The company’s efforts initially focused on buying wireless spectrum after receiving the Federal Communications Commission’s approval in 2024 to move forward with plans to offer a direct-to-phone version of its Starlink satellite internet service, in partnership with T-Mobile. SpaceX struck a $17 billion deal with EchoStar in 2025 and agreed this year to acquire a portfolio of low-band spectrum valued at $8 billion. Combining that wireless spectrum with mini cell towers should boost signals and end the dead zone problem, he said. According to Musk, the company has completed the design of what he described as “a micro cell tower thing that you just put on your roof, like a Starlink dish.” Musk, who has a history of missing his own production deadlines, demurred, saying the devices were “going into production, I think, next year.” The idea isn’t new, but it wasn’t clear until this week how much progress SpaceX had made toward developing the hardware. SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said during the company’s August earnings call that it wouldn’t use big cell towers and would instead deploy small, low-power cellular base stations. Even with this latest progress report, SpaceX appears to be still working out the details. Musk said one approach would be to bundle the small cellular base stations together with Starlink terminals. SpaceX’s plan to build a hybrid cellular-satellite network has fueled speculation, and even predictions, that legacy telecom companies could be in danger. But Musk doesn’t think so, because he expects an entirely new class of customers to drive demand for wireless bandwidth: AI. “I don’t think this means, like you know, AT&T, Verizon, or others go out of business or anything,” he said, adding that maybe they’ll lose some revenue. “But I actually think that the demand for bandwidth will be tremendous in the future, and a lot, and that bandwidth will be driven primarily by superintelligence and robots, and they’re going to need a lot more bandwidth than humans.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. articles.title: Want to see your live AI usage on your Mac’s icons? This clever new app lets you
articles.contentSnippet: IconSwapper brings your Mac's app icons to life with real-time data, animations, and playful customizations that make your desktop more fun.
articles.fullContent: There’s a new way to keep an eye on your AI usage and when your limits reset: by using your Mac’s app icons. Yes, really! Designer Michael Flarup has just launched a new Mac utility called IconSwapper, which lets you replace any app’s official icon with one of your own creation. While you can use this tool to change your icons’ appearance, design, shading, and more, one of the more interesting ways to use it is to swap the icons for AI apps like ChatGPT or Claude with versions that can display your live AI usage. Doing so is fairly simple, and you don’t have to be technically minded to get this to work. After installing the app on your Mac, you simply choose which application you want to create a “live” icon for — meaning one that responds to a particular app. Image Credits:IconSwapper Besides tracking AI usage in ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor, you can also create live icons for a number of the built-in Mac apps like Messages, Mail, Safari, Finder, Music, and others like Chrome and Spotify, but these configurations tend to be more fun than they are practical. For instance, you can configure Safari’s compass to follow things like page loads and downloads, or you can make it so that the Finder guy’s eyes follow your cursor around the screen. (That one is hilarious!) Image Credits:IconSwapper (screenshot) Of course, there are plenty of other ways to track your AI usage — you don’t need an icon to do that. You can track usage from your account or your harness, even from a fun little gadget. But tracking it from the icon adds a certain whimsy to your Mac desktop setup. (If your dock is crowded, note that you can also see your icon customizations from your tab bar as you switch apps.) Beyond live icons, you can also change what an icon looks like using IconSwapper’s built-in tools. There are a surprising number of built-in customizations that are as easy to use as clicking a few buttons or toggling a switch. IconSwapper also comes with a large library of alternative icons for every app that are already ready to use, or you can upload your own. Image Credits:IconSwapper Flarup is based in Copenhagen, where he runs a design studio, and he has been drawn to icon design and customization for years. He’s been making his own Mac icons since the early 2000s and even wrote a book about app icons that celebrates the work of designers. He had been working on a solution that would allow him to customize Mac icons, which had proven tricky because macOS has no official support for theming and protects its system icons. To work around this, he came up with a different technique that involves drawing directly on the icons without replacing them, allowing him to use shaders, motion, and display real data. Flarup tells TechCrunch that his renderer runs the icon artwork through custom Metal shaders in real time. Image Credits:IconSwapper “The breakthrough was figuring out how to send the Dock a bitmap for another running app and have it draw that frame itself,” he explained. “I spent a lot of time getting the artwork to follow the icon through all the little ways macOS moves it, from Dock magnification to the Command-Tab switcher. Once I had that working, I could make the icon react to whatever’s happening,” Flarup said. That lets users configure icons to do all kinds of fun, new things they never could before, like make light move across a gold icon as you drag your cursor over it, or animate an app’s icon while it’s thinking. “That opens up a lot of fun ways to make your Mac feel like yours. I’ve always felt the software we use every day could be a little more fun and a lot more personal,” he added. The app itself is a one-time purchase of $19 as a launch promo but will later sell for $29, its website says. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. articles.title: Meta’s new Muse Charm device may cost $300
articles.contentSnippet: Meta hasn't denied the reporting from The Information, saying only that it will "have more to share soon" about its upcoming AI wearable.
articles.fullContent: In Brief Posted: 1:58 PM PST · November 19, 2026 Image Credits:Meta/screenshot / Meta plans to charge $300 for Muse Charm, its upcoming Tamagotchi-like AI device that was teased at the company’s Connect event earlier this year, The Information has reported. When reached for comment by TechCrunch, a Meta spokesperson didn’t deny the claims, merely providing the following statement: “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.” So far, Meta has made a relatively successful push into consumer AI, launching Muse — its agentic helper — along with a variety of cute avatars that users can use to give the system more of a personality. Muse Charm, the company’s push into AI hardware, will allow users to carry a physical personification of its software around in their pocket (or potentially wear it around their neck), talking to it, asking it questions, and giving it commands. It remains to be seen whether customers will bite or not. AI wearables have had a rough go of it so far (here’s looking at you, Humane Ai pin), but companies continue to iterate on the concept in an attempt to break through to a broader audience. Indeed, $300 is arguably a pretty steep price for a product the size of a keychain, although it’s also a price point that’s in line with what other companies have been charging. The wearable launched by Friend — the AI startup whose device lets you text and talk to an AI persona — is currently retailing for $250. On the other hand, Amazon’s all-new Bee Frontier wearable AI device — which transcribes conversations and tracks tasks — lists for $75 and is currently on a Black Friday, 30% off sale of $52.49. Even with its $99/year subscription to let it tie into a user’s apps (photos, emails, etc.), it’s still far less expensive than Muse Charm.
